To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

tumor-specific mutations of CKIT and PDGFRA can be detected in plasma samples of GIST patients, and the detection of mutant fcDNA can be used as a biomarker to monitor disease course and response to therapy.

we were able to detect tumor-specific mutant DNA in the plasma of 15 of 39 patients with GIST harbored activating mutations of CKT or PDGFRA, irrespective of current treatment and disease status, which correlated with disease course and allowed the detection of resistance mutations.

we were able to identify and quantify tumor-specific DNA fragments in the plasma of 15 of 31 patients with GIST, and that the amount of tumor-specific DNA correlated with the disease status of these patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of biomarkers for gastrointestinal stromal tumor.

the identification of tumor specific biomarkers for the detection of minimal residual disease in patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) harboring activating mutations in the tyrosine kinases KIT or PDGF.

the detection of free circulating DNA (fdDNA) in plasma samples of GIST patients harboring activating mutations in the kinase domain of CKIT or in the kinase domain or the juxtamembrane domain of PDGFRA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this is a very interesting study, which shows that plasma DNA can be used to detect tumor-specific mutations.
the detection of circulating tumor DNA in plasma is a promising approach in the management of GIST.

the detection of mutant fcDNA harboring CKIT/PDGFR mutations in plasma samples of GIST patients can be used as a tumor-specific biomarker and that this approach might allow earlier treatment decisions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we were able to identify a new biomarker in GIST.
we were able to show for the first time that the detection of mutant free circulating tumor DNA (fcDNA) in the plasma of GIST patients is feasible.
we can detect tumor-specific mutant DNA fragments in plasma samples of 15 out of 38 patients (39%) with GIST.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have developed a new method to detect and quantify tumor mutations in the plasma.
the detection of tumor-specific DNA fragments in the plasma of a patient with GIST harbors activating mutations of CKit or PDGFRα allows a noninvasive and tumor-specific monitoring of the disease.
circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a biomarker that is very sensitive to the presence of disease.
